lessons.title: CPU tools: top, mpstat, pidstat, vmstat
lessons.goal:
Read the CPU time breakdown (user, system, idle, iowait, steal), find which process uses it, and tell CPU-bound from I/O-bound work.

Why it matters: `top` is on every machine, but its numbers have meanings you must know: 100% `us` is a different problem from 100% `sy` or high `wa`.

setup.note: Programs are small C files (gcc needed). perf, sysstat (mpstat, pidstat) are used; install with `dnf install perf sysstat`.

steps.title: The CPU time categories
steps.text: The kernel accounts every tick to one category: **us** user code, **sy** kernel code (system calls, interrupts handling), **ni** niced user code, **id** idle, **wa** idle while tasks wait for I/O, **hi/si** hardware/software interrupts, **st** *steal*: time the hypervisor gave to another VM. High `st` on a virtual machine means the host is overcommitted.

run.output: counters since boot (ticks): user 23818675 system 11233397 idle 332031576 iowait 30180154 steal 7560729

steps.title: A process using CPU
steps.text: We start a busy loop and look at it with `top -b -n 1 -p PID` (batch mode, one iteration, one process). `%CPU` is the share of one CPU.

run.cmd: sh -c 'while :; do :; done' & echo $! > busy.pid; sleep 2; top -b -n 1 -p $(cat busy.pid) | tail -n 2 | awk 'NR==1 {print $1, $9, $10, $12} NR==2 {print $1, $9, $10, $12}'

steps.title: Per-CPU with mpstat
steps.text: `mpstat -P ALL 1 1` shows each CPU separately. One saturated CPU with others idle means a single-threaded bottleneck (the average hides it).

steps.title: Per-process with pidstat
steps.text: `pidstat -u -p PID 1 2` samples one process: `%usr`, `%system` and `%CPU`. `pidstat -w` adds context switches: **voluntary** (the task blocked) and **non-voluntary** (the scheduler preempted it, a sign of CPU competition).

steps.title: Is it CPU-bound or I/O-bound?
steps.text: A CPU-bound task shows high `%usr` and few voluntary switches. An I/O-bound task shows low CPU, many voluntary switches and `wa` in the system line. Compare with a task that mostly sleeps:

run.cmd: kill $(cat busy.pid); sh -c 'while :; do sleep 0.01; done' & echo $! > sleepy.pid; sleep 1; pidstat -u -w -p $(cat sleepy.pid) 1 2 | awk '/Average/ && $4 ~ /^[0-9.]+$/ {print $0}' | awk '{print $4, $5, $8}' | tr '\n' ' '; echo; kill $(cat sleepy.pid)

steps.under: `top` and `mpstat` read `/proc/stat` (system-wide ticks) and `/proc/PID/stat` (`utime`, `stime` per process) twice and compute the difference. Accounting in ticks (usually 100 per second) is statistical: a task that runs for 1 ms between two ticks may be charged for none or for a whole tick. For precise per-event data use `perf`.

quiz.q: What does a high `st` (steal) value in a VM mean?
options: The hypervisor gave CPU time to other guests
quiz.explain: The VM wanted CPU but the host was busy.

quiz.q: One CPU is at 100% and seven are idle. `top` shows 12% for the whole machine. What does this suggest?
quiz.explain: Look per CPU with mpstat -P ALL.

options: The scheduler preempts the task: CPU competition
quiz.explain: The task was forced off the CPU.

quiz.q: Which tool samples one process's CPU use every second?

check.scenario: `top` shows `%Cpu: 5 us, 3 sy, 0 id, 92 wa`. What is the machine doing and what do you check next?
check.answer: It is almost entirely waiting for I/O (`wa`), not computing. Check `iostat -x 1` for the busy device (`%util`, `await`), `ps -eo pid,stat,wchan,comm | awk '$2 ~ /^D/'` for the waiting tasks, `iotop`/`pidstat -d` for who generates the I/O, and storage or NFS health.

lessons.title: perf: counting and profiling where the CPU time goes
lessons.goal:
Use `perf stat` to count events and `perf record`/`perf report` to find the function that burns the CPU.

Why it matters: `top` tells you *which process*; `perf` tells you *which function*. It is the standard tool for "why is this program slow" on Linux, without changing the program.

setup.note: Programs are small C files (gcc needed). perf, sysstat (mpstat, pidstat) are used; install with `dnf install perf sysstat`.

steps.title: A program with a hot spot
steps.text: `hot.c` runs two functions: `heavy` (square root and sine) and `light` (a simple sum). One of them takes almost all the time. Compile with `-g` and keep frame pointers so call chains work.

steps.title: perf stat: count events
steps.text: `perf stat` runs the command and prints counters: `task-clock` (CPU time), context switches, migrations, page faults, and (if the hardware allows) CPU cycles and instructions. A VM may not expose hardware counters; software ones always work.

steps.title: perf record: sample the program
steps.text: `perf record -F 499 -g` interrupts the program 499 times per second, and each time stores the **instruction pointer** and the **call chain**. Functions that run longer are sampled more often. The samples go to `perf.data`.

run.cmd: perf record -q -F 499 -g -o perf.data ./hot > /dev/null 2>&1; ls -s perf.data | awk '{print "perf.data written"}'

steps.title: perf report: the answer
steps.text: `perf report --no-children` lists functions by their **own** share of samples. The hot function is at the top. `--stdio` prints text instead of the interactive screen.
steps.after: Almost all samples fall in `sinf32x`, the libm sine function called from `heavy`. `light` is hardly visible. Without the profiler we might have optimised the wrong function.

steps.title: Who calls it?
steps.text: With call graphs (`-g`), the report also shows the chain of callers. `perf annotate` goes further and shows the hot instructions. For a running process use `perf top -p PID` or `perf record -p PID -- sleep 10`.

run.cmd: perf report -i perf.data --stdio --no-children --percent-limit 20 -G 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'main|sinf32x|heavy' | head -n 3 | sed -E 's/^[ |-]+//' | cut -c1-60

steps.under: perf uses the kernel's `perf_event_open` system call. The sampling interrupt comes from a **hardware performance counter** overflowing (cycles) or from a timer (`cpu-clock`) when counters are not available, as on many VMs. The kernel stores samples in a lock-free ring buffer shared with the `perf` process. Flame graphs (Brendan Gregg) draw the same data as a stack-based picture: wide boxes are hot.

quiz.q: What does `perf record -g` add compared to plain `perf record`?

options: Counts of events for a whole run
quiz.explain: Totals such as task-clock and context-switches.

options: So call chains can be unwound reliably
quiz.explain: Frame pointers let perf walk the stack.

quiz.q: Hardware counters are not available in a VM. What does perf use for sampling?

check.scenario: A service uses 80% CPU in production, you cannot restart it and you have no source. How do you find the hot function?
check.answer: `sudo perf record -F 99 -g -p PID -- sleep 30`, then `perf report --stdio --no-children | head -50` (or generate a flame graph). Symbols need debug info or at least unstripped binaries; for JIT languages use their perf map support. Sampling at 99 Hz has negligible overhead, so it is safe in production.

interview.q: What do us, sy, id, wa and st mean in top?
interview.a: User time, kernel time, idle, idle while waiting for I/O, and steal (CPU time taken by the hypervisor for other VMs). See [the lesson](#/lesson/42/top-mpstat-pidstat).

interview.q: How do you find a single-threaded bottleneck?
interview.a: `mpstat -P ALL 1` shows one CPU at 100% while the average is low; `pidstat -t` or `top -H` shows the busy thread.

interview.q: What are voluntary and non-voluntary context switches?
interview.a: Voluntary: the task blocked (I/O, lock, sleep). Non-voluntary: the scheduler preempted it, typically because other tasks wanted the CPU.

interview.q: How do you profile a running process without restarting it?
interview.a: `perf record -F 99 -g -p PID -- sleep 30` then `perf report`, or `perf top -p PID`. See [the lesson](#/lesson/42/perf-stat-record).

interview.q: Difference between perf stat and perf record?
interview.a: stat counts events over the whole run; record samples the instruction pointer and call stack to attribute time to functions.
A visualisation of sampled stacks where box width is the share of samples; wide boxes at the top are the hot functions.
